original_value: The increase in complex workpieces with changing geometries demands advanced control algorithms in order to achieve stable welding regimes. Usually, many experiments are required to identify and confirm the correct welding parameters. We present a method for controlling laser power in a remote laser welding system with a convolutional neural network (CNN) via a PID controller, based on optical triangulation feedback. AISI 304 metal sheets with a cumulative thickness of 1.5 mm were used. A total accuracy of 94% was achieved for CNN models on the test datasets. The rise time of the controller to achieve full penetration was less than 1.0 s from the start of welding. The Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) method was used to further understand the decision making of the model. It was determined that the CNN focuses mainly on the area of the interaction zone and can act accordingly if this interaction zone changes in size. Based on additional testing, we proposed improvements to increase overall controller performance and response time by implementing a feed-forward approach at the beginning of welding.

result.paraphrase: As workpieces become more complex and geometries change, advanced control algorithms are needed to maintain stable welding regimes. Identifying and validating the proper welding parameters usually requires many experiments. We describe a laser-power control method for a remote laser welding system that uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a PID controller and optical triangulation feedback. The material used was AISI 304 metal sheets with a combined thickness of 1.5 mm. On the test datasets, the CNN models achieved 94% total accuracy. The controller’s rise time to reach full penetration was under 1.0 s from welding start. To better interpret the model’s decisions, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was applied. The CNN was found to concentrate mainly on the interaction zone and to respond appropriately when the interaction zone changed in size. Further testing led us to propose performance and response-time improvements through a feed-forward approach at the start of welding.
